title: Website Operations Lab
short: Read the health report, then pick the next safe diagnostic
summary: A weekly health report for a small business site with six findings. Decide what comes first, what a 'successful' backup really tells you, and which next step is a read-only diagnostic rather than a change.

module.title: Generate a recurring inspection checklist for your own site

scenario: It is Monday morning. The weekly health report for Harbourline Physio's WordPress site has arrived. Everything in it was produced by read-only checks. You have an hour before the clinic opens and the receptionist starts relying on the contact form.

steps.title: What comes first?
steps.instruction: Two findings are urgent. Decide the order and be able to say why.

decision.question: First, in the hour you have:

options.label: The certificate. It expires in four days, auto-renew is 'enabled' but the log shows three consecutive failed renewals — so in four days the site goes down for every visitor, on a known date. The security update is second, today.
The security update to the forms plugin. Security always comes first.
The 404 spike — 312 errors is the biggest number on the page.

explain.correct: Priority is consequence × certainty × time. An expired certificate is a total outage for every visitor, and the renewal log makes it near-certain: three failures, four days left, 'enabled' meaning nothing. The security patch is genuinely urgent too and gets done in the same hour — but a vulnerability is a possibility and the expiry is a date.

wrong.security: Do it today — but a plugin vulnerability is a risk; a certificate expiring in four days with three failed renewals is a scheduled outage. Order by what fails hardest, soonest, most certainly.
wrong.404: 298 of 312 are one URL, /blog/feed — almost certainly a feed reader polling a URL that moved. Worth a redirect this week; nobody's site goes down over it.
wrong.form: Untested is not broken. It is the most valuable check on the list and takes two minutes — do it in this hour — but it is a diagnostic, not the emergency.

steps.title: What is the next safe diagnostic for the certificate?
steps.instruction: Observe before you change. The log says the http-01 challenge times out.

options.label: From outside the server, fetch http://harbourline.example/.well-known/acme-challenge/test and note what happens (timeout, redirect to https, 404). Then a dry run: certbot renew --dry-run. Nothing changes; both tell you exactly what is blocking the challenge.
Run certbot renew --force-renewal now and see if it works.
Switch the site to HTTP until the certificate is sorted out.
Reboot the server; renewals often fix themselves.

explain.correct: The log already names the symptom (timeout on the http-01 fetch, 'likely firewall'). The cheapest next fact is whether port 80 answers from outside at all. A dry run repeats the real challenge without touching the certificate. Both are read-only, both take a minute, and the answer tells you which change to make — usually a firewall rule or a redirect that fires before the challenge path.

wrong.force: A forced renewal repeats the same failing challenge and, with rate limits, can lock you out of retries for a week. You would be spending attempts to learn what the log already says.
wrong.disable: That converts a possible outage in four days into a certain security regression now, and breaks every https link to the site.
wrong.reboot: Nothing in the log points at the server being wedged. A reboot is a change with a visible outage and no diagnostic value here.

steps.title: What does '7/7 SUCCESS' mean?
steps.instruction: Read the log the report links to.

options.label: The files are being copied and the database is not — mysqldump is missing, so every 'SUCCESS' is a backup of the theme and uploads with no posts, pages, bookings or settings. Nothing is known about restorability until one is restored.
Backups are healthy: seven successes, 148 MB each.
The site can be restored to any of the last seven nights.

explain.correct: The line 'database: skipped' is inside a job that reports SUCCESS. On WordPress the database is the site; the files are furniture. This is the second lab on this site where a green backup line hides the fault, and it is not a coincidence — 'the job ran' is the most common thing a backup check actually measures. Fix: install mysqldump (or the platform's export), then restore one backup somewhere and open it.

wrong.ok: 148 MB of files and no database. Read the third line of each night.
wrong.restore: Restorability is established by restoring. Nothing here has been restored, and half of what would need restoring was never saved.

steps.title: The contact form, untested for 47 days
steps.instruction: The receptionist arrives in forty minutes.

options.label: Submit the form from a phone with a marker (a date-stamped string) and confirm the marked message arrives in the inbox it is supposed to reach. Record the time both ways.
Fetch the page and confirm it returns 200 with the form in the HTML.
Update the forms plugin first; the update is a security fix, and it will fix the form if anything is wrong.

explain.correct: A form check is a delivery check. The page returning 200 and the plugin being current both leave the actual question open: does a message sent now arrive where a human reads it? A marked submission answers it, takes two minutes, and — if it fails — is the most important finding of the week.

wrong.http: That proves the form renders. Forms that render and deliver nothing are the most common silent failure on small business sites.
wrong.plugin: Update it today — after the test. Testing first tells you whether the form was working before the update, which you need to know if it is not working after.

after.title: After: what happened in the hour
after.content:
07:12 external fetch of /.well-known/acme-challenge/test: 301 → https (a blanket redirect rule fires before the challenge path)
07:14 certbot renew --dry-run: same failure, confirmed cause
07:20 redirect rule given an exception for /.well-known/acme-challenge/ (one line, reverted if needed)
07:22 certbot renew --dry-run: success · 07:23 certbot renew: certificate renewed, expires in 90 days
07:30 contact form: marker OPS-2026-09-14-0730 sent from phone; received in reception inbox 07:30:48
07:35 forms plugin 3.4.1 → 3.4.2 on staging, form re-tested, then production; re-tested (marker …-0741)
07:50 mysqldump installed; manual backup with database; restore to scratch host opened: posts and settings present
08:00 /blog/feed → /feed redirect added; 404s to be re-read next week
Report updated with evidence for each line.

closing: Every change in that hour was preceded by a read-only look that made the change small and reversible. That is what the maintenance guide's weekly checklist is for, and what the report template's Evidence column enforces.
